title: Nothing Confirms Layoffs and Restructuring, Denies Plans to Exit Global Markets
excerpt: The London-based smartphone maker says it is reorganizing for its 'next phase of growth' while denying reports of pulling out of 12 markets — but the industry-wide memory crisis is forcing painful cuts across the board.
body:
• Nothing confirmed layoffs and team reorganizations on July 24, while co-founder Akis Evangelidis denied reports the company would exit 12 global markets.
  • Indian publication Digit reported Nothing is shutting down in 12+ markets including the Middle East, Japan, and parts of Europe, with global headcount cuts of up to 40%.
  • The global memory chip shortage — dubbed 'RAMageddon' — has driven component costs up roughly fourfold since September 2025, forcing Nothing to cancel its CMF budget phone line for 2026.
  • Nothing sold approximately 2 million units globally in 2025, but sustaining those volumes in 2026 is increasingly difficult as mid-range and budget smartphone segments contract sharply.

Nothing co-founder Akis Evangelidis took to X on July 24 to push back against reports that the London-based smartphone company was planning to pull out of a dozen countries. "FAKE NEWS… We are not shutting down any markets," he wrote, calling the claims "inaccurate reports."

But his post confirmed that layoffs are underway. Nothing is "reorganising" its teams, Evangelidis said, in preparation for its "next phase of growth," which includes the creation of an "AI-native business unit."

"Decisions that impact people's livelihoods are never taken lightly, and we know how difficult this transition is for our team members who are affected," he added.

What the Reports Claimed

The denial was a direct response to an exclusive report by Indian tech publication Digit, which cited multiple sources claiming Nothing was in the process of shutting down in 12 or more global markets. Those exits, according to Digit, include the Middle East, Japan, and parts of Europe. The report also stated that Nothing's global headcount would be reduced by 30 to 40 percent, with R&D teams — split roughly 70:30 between China and London — facing layoffs of around 50 percent and 30 to 40 percent, respectively.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2080985275681927267

Digit reported that Nothing's newest budget phone, the Phone (4b), had shipped approximately 20,000 units globally since its July 7 launch. Evangelidis countered that claim with different numbers, stating on X that the Phone (4b) had sold 29,537 units on day one alone, "breaking records in its price segment." The phone launched at $400.

Evangelidis did not directly address the specific headcount reduction percentages cited by Digit.

The RAMageddon Problem

Whichever version of events proves more accurate, the underlying pressure on Nothing is clear: the global memory chip shortage is reshaping the smartphone industry from the ground up.

Nothing CEO Carl Pei has been among the most vocal executives about the crisis. In a series of posts on X in June, Pei laid out the scale of the problem. Memory, he said, is now the single most expensive component in a smartphone, surpassing processors and displays, and can account for more than 50 percent of the total hardware bill.

"For Phone (4a), memory costs doubled between when we decided to build the device and launch, then doubled again in the months that followed."

— Carl Pei, CEO, Nothing

Memory prices have risen approximately fourfold since September 2025, according to Counterpoint Research, driven by AI data centres securing production capacity years in advance. Modules that cost under $20 a year ago could exceed $100 in premium devices by year-end, Pei warned. He predicted that manufacturers would need to raise prices by 30 percent or more, or strip specifications to survive.

The broader market data backs this up. IDC projects global smartphone shipments will decline 12.9 percent year-on-year in 2026 to 1.1 billion units — the lowest annual volume in over a decade. Smaller vendors are expected to bear the brunt of that contraction.

CMF's Collapse and Key Departures

Nothing has already felt the squeeze acutely through CMF, its budget sub-brand. In June, Evangelidis confirmed that the planned successor to the CMF Phone 2 Pro had been canceled outright. "We were working on a successor, but with memory prices where they are right now, we can't build a phone that feels like a genuine step forward at a price that makes sense for CMF," he wrote.

Producing a device with the same specifications as the CMF Phone 2 Pro — which originally retailed at $279 — would now cost roughly 50 percent more. The sub-Rs 20,000 segment in India where CMF competed fell 45 percent year-on-year in Q2 2026, according to Counterpoint. At least one device planned for CMF has been shifted to the main Nothing brand, where higher pricing is more defensible.

Himanshu Tandon, the executive who built CMF into one of India's most talked-about challenger brands and formerly served as India Head for Xiaomi's Poco, has also stepped down. His departure, combined with the product freeze, leaves CMF effectively dormant.

India: Bright Spot, Small Base

For Indian diaspora consumers and tech watchers, the picture is nuanced. Nothing posted 105 percent year-on-year growth in India during Q2 2026, according to Counterpoint Research, driven by the Phone (4a) series and a high-profile IPL sponsorship with Royal Challengers Bengaluru. But that figure excludes CMF, which was spun off as a separate entity, and represents growth off a relatively small base. Nothing sold approximately 2 million units globally in all of 2025.

India remains one of Nothing's strongest markets, but the company is contracting everywhere else. And it is not alone: OnePlus has begun exiting North American and European markets entirely as part of a broader restructuring at parent company Oppo, with a full global withdrawal — excluding China — expected by 2027.

What Comes Next

Nothing has signaled it will not release a flagship smartphone in 2026. Its immediate product lineup is narrowed to the Phone (4a) series and the Phone (4b), alongside audio products. The company has also leaned into lifestyle marketing, appointing pop star Charli xcx as a global brand ambassador and shareholder.

Whether the restructuring amounts to a strategic refocus or the early stages of a broader retreat depends on variables Nothing cannot control — chiefly, when memory prices stabilize. Chinese chipmakers CXMT and YMTC are reportedly stockpiling DRAM that could flood the market in 2027, but the shortage is expected to persist through at least Q1 2028, according to industry sources cited by Gadgets 360. Until then, the squeeze on mid-range and budget smartphone makers will only intensify.
